THE CHRISTMAS Ross.—The Christmas rose ie one of the sasisat plants e, grow, but when left entirely to itself it Bowers late, mid the flowers are much torn and dlecoloured by the unkind weather that usually prevails in its dowering season. The plant is • alive of Southern Europe, and needs for its perfect development better conditions than are usually eecured for it in English gardens, more especially as it dowers at a time of year when the dements are in a mood to make war upon every green herb, and bar away the one last leaf that still bangs upon the tree. To put this plant inn com- mon border is not quite fair to it. A sheltered nook ehould be cboaen, and a plot of gronnd prepared by draining it thoroughly, unlest it is naturally well drained aireadygan' by deep digging and liberal manuriog.—Familids 00 Power& _

• OLD NAN. roe WattrLovrets.—The common name of the plant walliiewer is, of course, bestowed upon it from its being aoeseentially a lover of old walls; but we sometimes find St referred ten, the gilliflower, or willefer, a corroption of the French girojUer and Italian garofpno. We need scarcely remind any who read these realm-kg that the etymology of our language ILIA In mediaeval limed in a very chaotic state, and we find the plant appearing in eariou old authors as the gilotre, the gyllofer, jerenouris, and gariatilus—all more or less corrupt renderiuge of the Latin Caryophollurn, aflame h.towed on it from its clove-like odour. The name was, however, originally bestowed on the true dove, a SpeCiON of pink ; and while wale of our earlier writers refer to this ll- tee plant as the gillofer, later authors have transferred LIM name to tile wallflower. —Forel/ ear Mid Flowers. KINONESA AND PATIANCE.—Mr. E. Powell writes sugges- tively to the Aural Nov Yorker of a "spoiled" cow re- formed by moral auaaion i—"Comhtg home to farm on a vacation, after nearly a year's absence, fly' non' said 10 1110, ' you will have to sell that pet Ayrshire heifer. She is a terrible creature ; we can do nothing with her.' At milking time, I found they had her with a rope around her horns, in lietween does bars, aud then stout pins before and behind her hind legs. One switched off flies, while another milked. She made it lively, however, to spite of bars, pine, pegs, ropes, and men. It looked like a bed case. Iler eyes were full of mischief. The next day I had her led out on the lawn of nice grass for a good meal. The next day she seas Jet loose in the yard, when I took a rope to the gate, held it up, and caused her to come and let me put lion, promising hero good thne on the lawn. It woo at least a half lionea work of quiet, persistent waiting and talking. But she was slowly coming to the point of yieldiag. At last she held See head quietly down close M front of roe, and not till then did I yield one inch to her. She most submit before she couldhave the coveted grass. Then lied her out at once and gave her a good time. The result was that in three weeks the could be milked anywhere on the lawn without the least danger." CIIEDDAN Cxxe,..—Archde:icon Denison's "Notes on Cheese-making" haa been supplemented by a letter in reply to a gentleman who het written to him on the subject. The Archdeacon writesai follows Where farmers hitve corns to know that theee factories area great mistake, as I have always judgisl them to be, they are recalling checae-making into their oWn families, which was the way in which all good Cheddar cheese toed to he made, and must be made if it is On preserve its character and its price. /loam making and no artificial drying are the two principal elements of good che.e-making. lair almoat inconceivable that any farmers in the Cheddar cheese country should have thrown into the ditch all their valuable monopoly by allowiag themselvee to be deceived by the American example into artificial drying and rapid sale. A real Cheddar sheuld not be eiten under eighteen months from the date of mtking, and is best at two years from it. No American or factory-made cheese smells sweetly after six months, when it is a race between the men and the maggots. The public' generally have been taken In beeanse ninety-nine out of., hundred why buy cheese never buy a whole cheese, halo hunch of cheese, and then eat it up before they find out how badly made and how nasty it is. There is no country in Europe, or out of it, that eau make prime Cheddar cheese except Somerset, and it iA the worst folly to go and throw away, a monopoly, 'wing a natural gift. We had better go back and, if need be, live on bread and water two years, that in the third year we and our custontera may be able once maroon live on bread and red Cheddar cheeeea Them is re tretter food in the world—few foods no good, and we have beta throwing it all away like idiots.

I Mr. Sheldon's ininrenth;;; -La--;;;;;ctive publication, 1" Dairy Ferining,” ha a now reached the 16th part. It , contains neatly-coloured charts, givine the distribution of I the dairy industries of the United Stains. The letterprena of thin instilment of a valuable work treats of town and villa &drying, and of the Dairy Farming of Ireland. From Owe take the following account by Mr. R. Baster, of his dairy operations at Sr. Anne's 1,1111: .... . . . .

'll;farm is situated eight mile, front the city of Cork, and coneists of about 700 acres, princii,ally light land, red sandstone o,lthlittion. Two hundred acres have beet, drainel, rocks removed, and aubmil,d antler the Board of Works, and I are at present engaged in draining AO acres of ' flat alluvial bottom reeling on gravel, which I expect will turn out well. I grow about 25 acres of green crops each year, the larger portion ...angels, which are always a heavy crop, and five acres of forage crops. I manure the green ' crops with 30 loads per acre of farmyard manure made in a , covered shed (one load of which 1 consider apial to two of a.meo made in the ordinary way, exposed to the open air), and 6ewt. of superphosphate made as follows .—The boner are bought whole :and the labourers bre.tk them by contract, on wet days and winter eveninga, into half-inch bones, which are afterwards dissolved in sulphuric acid. The stock consists of 400 Shropshire sheep, 100 head of dry cattle,and 40 dairy cows. The dairy stock consists, principally, of three-taw. pureebred Shorthorns, a few pure-bred ditto, and three Berry, ; the latter give milk nearly as rich and as , highly coloured as that of Alderneys, and they have the • great advantage of being extremely hardy. The dairy is in connection with St. Anne's Hill Hydropathic Entabliah- ment, and a large quantity of fresh milk and butter ere required all the year round. In order to keep up the supply of these articles, some of the cows calve in autumn aud winter, but the greater proportion in spring. They are fed as follow, —Spring.—On the pasturee by day, noosed at ' night, getting each day Intone of mangeis per cow, will, a fair allowance of hay, and every evening a mixture of 211 cs. decorticated mke, Ilb. crushed Indian corn, and 111, bran, made into., mucilage with boiling water, and given warm. Suntatri..—On the pastures day and night; one feed of green foal each day, as the successive crops of rye, vetches, or , trifoliem come in. Autenm.—By day principally in the after-grasi, by night in the pastures ; mch evening a feed . of cabbage, and the cows on full milk a mixture of cake as above. friater.—Same as Spring. Great cleanliness is observed in the dairy management the milkers Are obliged an wash their hands, and the herdsmen to sponge the cown' udders before each milking. Each now in namberel, creel the milk ,tccurAtely measured once a week ; 20 have cont- . pleted their se.on's milk to January Ist. The average of milk per sow has been 632 gallons ; the highest 063 gallon. —front a three-partn-bred Shorthorn, ten months' milking, bred on the farm the lowest 563 gillone—from a half-bred three-year-old heifer, nizio months' milking, purchased ea a yearling. The averago percentage of cream h. been 14degs. when getting cake, Ildegs. not getting cake; highest per- centage I7degs., from a three-year-old three-par.-bred ShorMorn. It woe found in general that the larger the quantity of milk given, the lower was the percentage of ! cream. The average peld of butter has been, for each 10) gallons of milk net 35tha. for npring and winter, and 3011.5. for snmmer and autumn ; the milk is set in galvanized iron • yen.. for 24, 36, or 46 hours, according to the ne.ore of the , year—generdly 30 in summer, except in very hot neither, and 42 in winter. In cold wmther the dairy is heated by ntraneofaaere.tllfarreatreean,l thre placed under me corner of it, and in kept at a uniform temperature of from 4fidegs. to 50,tegs. The creme is warmed to .t temperature of 5-Ideas. ; before being put into the churn, and the agitation of churn- .' leg brings it np to °Mega, at which the bent remits are , obtained. Experimentn were tried during the late cold ' . I weather, and it wan found that the heating of the dairy and I the cream before churning increased the return hf butter fully 20 per cent. ; the quality Waa better, and it took a! . much shorter time tn churn than when put in cold. The ! , chum need is an 801 b. barrel-churn, turned by hand ; 40 minutru is the general time 'then in chanting. The butter . le handled ac little as posnible in the washing about lib. of ; salt is put to 501ba. of butter for the roll butter. A con- I siderable quantity of batter is mot to Dahlia every week in rolls. ; each lb. is folded in manlier, and packed in traye lea wooden case. In May and June, when the butter in plentiful, cement it is firkined for the Cork butter-market, when 31be. of silt are pot to the bib. firkin ; it obtaine time term " superfine quality," which is a new brand eatablished within the last two years in the Cork butter-nmarket. This quality is a mreful mlection from the best of the umild-cored, , and commands about 2d. a lb. over the price of the first quality. The merchants tell me the demand for it exceeds . the supply." Greater in Ireland even than in England is there need for improved dairy utensils and more careful treatment of milk, cream, and butter I yet it is true that nmmy of the more advanced frith dairies will mmpare not uolavour- . ably with corresponding onea in England, m far, that is, as succe.ful practice is concerned, and in this I.es the chief , merit of nuch plmen. It is at the small farms, md among the cottiers who milk only one or two cowa, that the dairy accommalation and equipment may be described 0 deploy- • ably bad : sanitary matters generally are at a low ebh ; the cowelleds and dung-heaps are absurdly time to the door and windows of the home : the milk is too often kept in the general living room of the family, or in a closely adjoining one into which the reeking smoke from the peat fire has the greite.nt freedom to enter; and the general surromdinge Cr. , anything but comlucire to cleanlinees. There in, however, in the present day a widenpread arid earnest effort being mode by many prominent n.en, who deserve well of their . country, to educate the rising generation,and all others who may care to learn, in the art and science of improved sys- tems of dairy manmement ; and it is mtisfactory to know . that the result of these efforta is already seen in a marked improvement in the average quality of the butter of some dlstricte in Ireland. We tract this reform will go on spread- , ing and deepening. until the habit, of the penile have , become imbued with a spirit of friendly emulation, and the • production of first-class butter is the rule and not the excep- tion in the Emerald Isle. In the re-arrangement of the Munnter Model Farm province a made torn thorough and : practical course of instruction in both outside and inside , dairy management. The training of the male pupils will extend over two sessions of four md a half month, each, et the very moderate fee of £7 10s. per annum, for which sum , the Boanl id Education provides the pupils with everything except clothing. In the months of Jan.ry and July, at , which period, no mine pupils will be resident at the Institu- tion, farmers' daughters and deiryrmids will be admitted as , pupils at an equally maierate lee, and placed under the care • , etc matron who is distinguished as a maker of price butter. , We hope to eee other imtitutione of this kind rising up in vtriona parte of the comtry, became we are soured theie Winona for good will be ennernoin.

Tux ERICHRON TORTHHO.—The New York paper. give further particulars concerning the invention of Capt. John Ericsson of a remarkable engine of naval w irfare, before which iron arrnour is rendered practically useless for slope of war. The weight of the projectile, including the piston, was 1,291 pounds, its diameter 15 inches, and its length 19 Ted. At Ito head it carri., as an explosive, A charge of dynamite weighing 2501 b., a cant-iron armature being affixed to the tail in order to balance the weight of the dynanalle. It Is shaped almost exactly like an enormous cigar, and, rushing through water point foremost, would suggext that rather than anything else. Captain Ericsson says the initial velocity with which his torpedo leaves the gun is at the rate of lt3o miles per minute. Of course this cannot long be maintained in such a medium an nater. The cap.in fires his torpedo n ith gunpowder. Ile says that the substitution of powder fur comprersed air in propelling sub- merged torpedoea ie the most important advance in that science which has recently been made. He computes, from the force of the charge, that there in not an iron ahip ' existence that could 'withstand the ahock of die explosion of the tremendous dynamite charge with which his cigar- shaped projectile le loaded. Tux Mons, awn raw WEA.ELL.-1, ice popular belief that weather alters, for the worm or the better, with the changes of the moon. If there were any truth in this 11u. tion, it would be easily .tablished by the accurate omen. vatiom of modem wiener. Mr. (flashier of the Royal Ob- servatory, exantimd the records kept there during twenty years, and he sq. Changre of weather have been as frequent at every age of the moon as when she WM seven, fourteen, terentymne, or twenty-eight days old; therefore she cannot have ball the slightest influence over any ul them." Other scientific observers have found changes a, marked about the first and third quarMrs as about new or full moon. In fact there is no conetant influence exertnl either in the weight or moisture or other quality of the at. moaphere on which weather depends. The notion of the moon's influence if a relic of superstition which attributed to the heavenly bosher a powerful influence over homes affairs. The belief is held chiefly by farmers, who, haying heard of changen at the new or fall moon, are very keen te expect them. When the coincideece ocean, as it must do occasionally by the law of probabiliti., their belief is strengthened. But they do not note with equal certainty the more frequent occasions when the coincidence fails ; aist when the season is favourable, the subjmt probably pasees without observation of any kind. The changes of the moon being continuous, it ia a priori improbable that an unusual influence should be exerted at the arbitrary periods of the full and new DlOOll, or the quarters, and science gives no support to the popular nothm.—Gisure flour. UNSINRAB. SIII..—The problem of rendering Mains Leo sinkable has from the earliest times received careful atten- tion from inventors and others, and various proposal°oe for effecting this object have been advanced from time to time, although, so far as we are aware, vote of them have ever been introduced into practice. 'Thin question has found another advocate in Mr. Lamb, of 4, Finsbury-circus, Lon- don, who has had a steam launch built to illustrate his system. This launch was inspected and a short run was made in her on Friday week at North Woolwich by a party of gentlemen interested in steam navigation. The principle consists in attaching to the sides of the hull of a vemel series of flat airdight met 111 ic cylinders or drums, the inner heads of which are built Into and form part of the framing and inner chin of the vessel. Them drums project on either side of the ship, and are c.o.f in, the under sides of the casings normally resting upon the surface of the water, and becoming slightly immersed under a load. The moult is a light &might with a great freeboard, and it is claimed that a greater stability under canv_s and a higher rate of speed under steam or sail are thereby attained, besides eeveral other contingent advantag.. The system is illustrated by means oft curd-built steam launch, 371 t. long oft. deep, an-d sft. Bin. beam internally. Shellae seven cylinders fitted on , each side, each cylinder being 31t. 6in, in diameter and Ift. • din. deep, and which give her a width on deck of 9ft, veer all. She drew, 21t. of water without her load, and hm a freeboard of 41t. The principlen of the system And the con. struction of the launch, which has no pretensions to beauty, ! were explained to the visitors during a short run, in which , a fair speed was maintained, the vessel moving very steadily. , There can be no queation of the safety of such a vessel under !most circumetanses as regards her immunity from sinking. although in applying the prhiciple in practice several goes- , Cone of detail will have to be met which have not been eon- , sidered in the launch in question. It is, however, only fair to state that the vessel is the first of its kind, and as far is , only experimental.—Times.

TR, Flri-Mrs Or Pottrraverrr ON Vrowe&MON—A few yr ir..• A,zo a remarkable occurrence in connection with injninooeletiofl led ton discovery which not only an. 'gems iiviu fully and clearly the occasional deleteriosta effects to planta teamed upon galvanised iron wire, but at the same tune it bas thrown loner light upon the laws of growth and distr.., and mrvm to elucidate a class iihe- nomena which had been previously altogether imumprelien. sible. A latge plant case on a bronzed stand, purchased from one of the first houses in London, aipl pi fitted with ferns by Mr. Kennedy, late of Covent Garden Market, was taken to Queen Anne-street, Cavendish-square, and placed in a situation in every w iy boo:amble to the ferns, but, strange to nay, instead of their flourishing, nr even contitin- ing in a fairly heathy condition, they all died. Attributing this, an One would n aurally, to mismanagement, the case was cleaned and replenished, hat only to esperienie a Bind- lar disappointment. It then became evident that xime un. naual condition must pertain to the case itself, serving to effect this destruction, and on clmer examination this was discovered. 'The case and framework being constructed of sine, and the broosed table of cot iron, neither the under aurface of the former nor the upper surface of the latter having been paintid, the two metal. were in contained hence a gaiVsnie aelion WAS set up between them. Now as the uninitiated reader may ho soopticol se to any pmeible influence to any practical extent from the mere contact of two dissimilar metals, let him place the end of a zinc tally upon the tip of his tongue, and one bow nit pair of common scimors under the tongue, and then bring the other bow to touch the zinc so that the two memls much esch other at one end at the mme time the moist tongue touches the two metals at the other end. At the moment of bringing them together a pmuliar saltieh tpste nih be experienced and re- pmted every time the metals are separated mil brought to- gether again. But now substitute a piece of silver—a half.crown—for the iron of the scissore under the tongue, and &much more perceptible effect will be produce]. Such, then, beim, the effect of the contact of the nine cm, with its iron stand, the obvious remedy Was to separate them by the insertion of insulating strips of woiden laths. 'lids was immediately 11 el recourse to, and in every few hour, the pLants, losing this galvanic influlnce, had assumed quite it different appear ince, and soon acquired a healthy luxuri- ance. Doubts being expressed whether it were possible that such apparently insignitleant means could have alone been the cinfie of the mischief, and nothing short of ocular evidence being convincing, the wooden laths were removed, and the mse, lull of hmithy term, wan thus again subjectsd to the galvanic action as it had been originally. On the billowing morning, or after about twent,four hours, the plants were dull and drooping, mildew bad appeared, and the case looked unnaturally moist. The next twenty-four j hours, however, brought matters to a crisis. Fronds were decaying and had become covered with fungoid growths, festooning from one to mother like cobwebs ; whilst the whole interior, both plants and soil, emitted most powerfully , the peculiar mushroom odour, in addition to which various minute fungi had sprung up in the vegetable remains eon- i stituting the soil below. Thin evidence having been :weep- I ted as sufficiently conclusive, the laths were replaced to as to destroy the galvanic actim and render the case innocuous • as before. On eAnnining it some few hours afterwards the change that had Mann place created no little astonish nent. Elardly a tr.:, of the former cobwebby appearance was to be eruec all the fungi had been dried up .ind had dimp. , peared, and the atmosphere within had become clear and Icy. It is now evident that galvanised wire, havirig an ex- ternal surface of sine, when fastened with iron nails most inevitably be equally galvanic in its effmts, yet when the f satenings are galvanised too the whole is rendered perfectly Moos-nom like the insulated plant cam. It la only when dimimilar metals are in contact with each other that the , wire becomee hurtful.— W. K. Bridgman, in Journal of • Horticulture.

As for myself, in my name and in that of my two sons, it is enough for me to notice once again the diversity of our policies." PARIS, Tueslay.—The Government took no measures to-1 day against the religious communities. Numbers of people continue to congre,ate in front of the various convents in Paris. The Carmelites of Filmy, who received orders on Saturday last to vacate their imastry, are now taking legal proceedings against M. Andrieux, the prefect of police. It . is announced that several more magistrates have resigned in consequence of the action of the Government in regard to the religious orders. N. Felix Pyat, proprietor and editor of the Commune, KIS been condemned in Contunacians to two year.' imprisonment ends fine of 1,000 francs in consequence of a series of articles defending regicide having appeared in his journal. M. Robert, the manager of me Commune, has also been sentenced to six months' imprisonment and a tine of 1,000

--;;ts,Wednesday.—A telegram received here this after- noon front Marseilles announces that the police have received orders to disperse groups of people who have collected near the approaches to the Capuchin Convent. Wednewley.—The Carmelites were expelled from their establishment in this town this morning. The pollee authorities were obliged to force the doors in order to effect an entrance Into the building. A number of gendarmes sod • battalion of infantry had also to he Summoned to maintain order in the vicinity of the establishment. •""•'•'"'"''•".

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 23, 1880.

Tux news which comae from South Africa is not of the moot pleseant or reaaturing character. The Ba.to muddle is being fought out to the bitter end, and the Cape Government, regardlene of the discoun- tenetce of the Englieh Cabinet, are bent upon com- pelling the Bunt., who hitherto have lived at pm., to yield to the caprice of isarmament. tin - ne emery newt have ftom the outeet held this war to be, we contoer to the experience of a feeling of grati- fication that the troops of the Colonial Government have, in engagements with the Smut., proved victorious. Had the engagements ended otherwiee, the worsting of the Colonial forces would probably have been an encouragement to other tribes to aasume • hcetile attitude, mato conbibute to an increase of the perplexities of the Cape Government bean extent to call for the reluctant but notice interference of the mother country. The Buntou have ill a few slight skinniehee proved themselves • de- termined and valiant raw ; but, if we are to give full credence to the reports trans- mitted by telegraph a mere handful of Colonial troops have auceeeded in patting a large army of Baeutoe to rout. Some time ago we reported in the Examiner that Colonel Carrington, with a few hun- dreds of men of the Cape Mounted Rifles, had been eurrounded at Mafeteng by 7,000 Basutos and abut up in their etronghold without supplies. Col. Clarke was then etated to be col looting reinforeemonta at Wapener, and i waa intended to lespateh these morose the boric from the Orange Free Siete to the sestina.. of Colonel Car- rington. The latter, however, found himself in desperate atraita, and we are told that on the 15th September he sallied out with his troops, and forced the Baautos to beat • retreat. Instead of the Basuto., however, numbeting 7,000, they had dwindled down to 1,000; and there are all the particulars we have yet been favoured with an to the engagement on the 15th. Where the 6,000 had disappeared to, or why they had disappeared the menage ie silent; and we are left to conjecture that their withdrawal was • part of some ...gin movement on the part of the Basuto chiefs. Mail not improbable, eing that on the 21s0 of Sep- tember the Colonial ride, and police, to the number of 400 fell in with a party of 7,000 Bunt., under the aommand of Lerothodi, one of the chide. The ac- count of the battle that ensued and to rmult is sur- rounded with considerable ampicion, although that account comes from the colonial force., who claim • bloodiest. victory. We are asked to believe that the swot:inter was a desperate one, and that whilst the Baattos were elain right and left by the 400 the 7,000 Baeutoo did not [mewed in killing • angle one out of the mere handful oppoe,ed to them. There is • oonfeasion that four of the colonial party were wounded, and that it was impoasible to count the the number of Basuton who were slain owing to their companions carrying them away as they were struck down by the bullets from the colonial riflee and police. We cannot but feel there has been a eup- preeedan of truth in relating the etory of the engage- ment, on the 15th and 21s1, and that the situation is not one of the meat comforting for the Cape Govern- mont. The Getout*tu may flatter themselves with the idea that hae been too often maned in this country tbst they can quickly throah all comers into subjeo- tion, but we fear they will discover they have lit a torah that will not be speedily extinguiehed. Since writing the above intelligenoe h. been re- ceived that on l'unday last, Colonel Clarke relieved the Imprisoned garrison under the command of Colonel Carrington at Mafeteng, the inveetment by the B.utos, notwithstanding the reported suoceasful sally of Colonel Carrington, haviug remained un- broken. General Clarke appears to have etarted from Wapener, which I. only fifteen miles from Maleteng, with 1,660 officere and men and two gone, and about ale thousand of the aoldien were mounted. His pro. green we, contented by the Neut., by whom he was attacketlwith vigour. The engagement that followed continued for some time. Eventually the natives ' ware defeated, and communication was at once opened with Maieteng. The Bunton are reported to have loot 300 men, whilst the colonial force had 26 men killed and 10 wounded. The Coloniste are naturally highly elated in having ovecoome the Bunke without the aid of English troops, and it will be for the Home Government to see that the victors do not use their awe., an • mune to the Imposition of 1110•81lrall of tyranny. Whilst Catewayo is doing penance in the air- ...crib.' area in which he to perrcitted to move, it ia alleged that the grave of his father, Panda, haa been rifled, and that Chief John Dunn, who would wen to be fulfilling the old adage concerning the putting of a beggar on horeeback, 13oa been airing hie grievaneru through the columns of a Natal journal in reel.ct of chic allegation. Bishop Coloneo ie the authority from which the charge of this outrage springs, and though Chief John Dunn denies that he wee prevent when Panda's gear. was rifled, the bishop reiteratee the charge and avows his medium to prove it. Dunn does admit that • white man had informed him that, having on the same evening on which Panda', bones were carried off been told of the outrage, he visited the King's rave on the following morning, and "now that it had beau ' vidated.' " Dunn, is in high dudgeon with Dr. Colense. "I in- tend," he says, "punishing any of my eubjecta I find negotiating with the Bishop without my knowledge, lbe It is not for peaceful purpose.." What the nature of the punishment ie that he means to deal out to those of hie " subjects " who dare behold communion with Bishop Colon., Chief John Dunn does not venture to tweet, bat hie angry letter to the Natal journala carries with it a a.picion that Dunn conuives himecif lobe • mighty potentate, and that there is jut groan& for believing that uniale he i reminded in unvarnished term, who and what be Is, and • check put upon hi. ambition, he will give trouble some day to the Government that put him in his prevent station. He write, that he hue demanded from ono of his " subjecte " an explanation of at. conduct in taking part in a recent deputation of Zulus to Pietermaritzburg without having lest obtained hi. permission. That deputation visited the Lieutenant-Governor of Natal, in order to make him acquainted with the views of the Zulus concerning their present position; and the quution consequently aria, whether theta natio., even though they be " enbjects " of Chief John Dunn, are not at liberty to oommunicate with the Queen's represent Mi. in Natal without first making leave of the man against whom, perhapo, they may have grievant. to allege. What Chief John Dunn I. aiming at may not be

quite clear, but it le significant that ha should date lea letter from Dunnsland, a ramie hitherto unknown in Zululand. Chief John Doom Om either a Britialt subject 081 or he has come to stand ors different I relation to the Britiah Government than he wen supposed to do when he wee mode Chief. If he 61 aiming at higher game than a Chieftainship under the British Government, troubles in South Africa will not I be lessened.

Tim Bishop of Salisbury has evidently formed some curious notions as to when the clergy in his, Reggae may sin or not sin in carrying out the pro- I visions a the new Burial Act affecting the interment I of Nonconformism in Church graveyards. He advises them to register the tenants of Nonconformists as it Is order-el by the law of the land, and, not being easeful, should be complied with. Bat the tolling of the Cherch bell before or after the funerals of Non- , oonformiste is a totally different matter, and he re- I commends his ckggis ;jot to tolerate this being done. We suppose the right rev. crel•to thi••• itsaorileg. that a bell whish proclaims thee • Chur•h‘••• gone over to the majority should be used to eio:Rire to the outer world that a Dissenter has given up the ghost. There are but few out of every thousand of Churchmen able to say why a Church bell is tolled at all on the ommion of n 1 unerel, and if they were asked they would jump at tho suggestion that it is to impart to the ceremony additional solemnity, and to increase the foe. the. all into the lap of the clergyman, the clerk, or the sexton. It is one of those superstitions which the Protestant Church of England took over with the ROLOOn ClithOlii• edifices at the time of the Red ormation, and, as the " roaming hell" served • procti.l turn, it lies Wen retained in the serviee of the Establiohment on, d it has, in the opioniofi of the Bishop of Saliebury, tmome endowed with so much sanotity that it wouLl '`n sinful to apply it to each hose uses as agitating its Mauer on the death of a Di.- seater. The "passing boil" was intraluced to be- speak the prayers of the ministers aud all good Christians for a soul just depatting, and to drive away the evil spirits who wore oupposed to await about the house of a person at the point of death, ready to seise their prey, or to molest and terrify the mut in it. passage. If the right rev. preLote of Salisbury recogniaeo at this day the same objecte the andante had in intro- duoing and continuing the " paseing bell," it is evi• dent he is anxious that evil spirits shall be allowed to terrify the mule of Diameters, and that be considers it his business., • Minister of the Savionr to see to it that they are terrified, if the silencing of "passing hells" when Diameters die can give • dear °ourso to sprites to exercise their weird dila.. But we fancy there will not be much trembling among the DN. meters Dr. Phillimore, a high authority en cheirch matters, however, has come to the rescue, and, if his atatemmits in • letter to the Times are to be aoeepted as a correct reading of canon law, the rifest rev. prelate of Salisbury must feel that before he again advises his clergy upon the tolling of the' paosiog bell" he had better look to the c.oas for an increase of knowledge. Dr. Phillimore sey...—" There meme to be some doubt whether the clergy should allow • bell to be tolled at funerals taking place under the new Burials Act. Ono of the bishops lately observed theta would be ungracioto to refuse. I venture to think it would also be illegal. By the 671 h canon, ' when any is passing out of this life • bell shall be tolled And after the party's death, if it

so fall out, there shall be rung no more than one abort peal, and moother after the burial.' No reference is made to any kind of service, and doubtless them peele may be rung at the burial of the excom- munioated, the unbaptized, or suicides. How much rather, then, at burials under the new dot? Moreover, the ' passing bell,' which now takes the plsoe of the one short peal immediately after the death is known to the sexton, must almost of neces- eity be rung before the friends have elected to avail themselves of the Act. Would it not be at least un- remonable to forbid the acme bell to be tolled at the f aneral a day or two later? The bells are parish pro • perty, but the custody thereof belongs to the church • wardens."

A Connaseowontrt, writing from South Africa, state. that Cetewayo is confined to Cape Town Castle, and that the only chance he hoe of getting fresh air and exercise is he walking on the ramparts. Sir Bartle Frere, who is responsible for the war which reduced Cetewayo to his pre- sent position, actually repeated a French misaionary to take • deputation of Basuto, to see the fallen log, as a warning of what IVY likely to be their chieFs fate. It is, perhaps, considering all things, undesirable that our authorities should attract as little attention as poeeible to the royal prisoner in Cape Town Castle. But is it not possible to Concede to him a greater range of freedom? Ceterrayell offence consisted in defending his country against an unpro- voked and unjust invasion. Ilia people vrere slain, his lands were ravaged, and he was captured and imprisoned as conquered King. Re, however, knows, that the war which deprives' hi m of his royal position was proclaimed as unjust by the very Government which ordered him into custody for doing his duty, and his experience of the justice of a civilised Government is not likely to intensify his esteem for the fair dealing which the white man boesta of having a love for. If lois release is held to be inexpedient, is there any reason why should not have more freedom than he now enjoys? Langalibalelo, the leader of the Kaffir outbreak of 1873, was confined on Robben Island in August, 1874, but in the following year he was released and placed under surveillance t colony. Surely Cetewayo is not held to be more dangerous:than Langalibatele was, and there in no excuse for extending different treatment to him.

IT would be vain to deny that there is a reign of terror ire the Sister Isle, and that the Government can no longer permit agitatore to foment passions tha assamina- Cons and place peaceable citizens in perpetual fear. Whilst the existing law is held sufficient to meet offences against life and property, there is of course, no necessity for the miming and enforeement of coercive measurea curbing liberty l of speech within the ordinary limite of freedom either in prewribrd districts or in a whole kingdom. Lawless agile. tators, ae a rule, aspire to become martyrs that they may rise in the estimation of those whom they succeed in mis- leading. The Government have avoided making martyr*, and the lomentors of anarchy have not acquired that im- portance of notoriety with lawless mote they would other- wise have gained. The Government, whilst recognising that the masses of Ireland have much to be aggrieved at in the present uneatisfactory state of the land laws, have evinced a determination to enforce a respect for the laws as they mint; but they have been unwilling to not legal machinery in motion until satisfied that the prawns against whom it might be necessary to direct it could be brought under its operation without risk of failure. The law officers of the Crown at Dublin have for some timo been engaged in pm. paring information against land agitators who are recognised leaders of the National Land League, and it is now an- nounced that tee Government have resolved to institute proceedings for sodition and conspiracy against thirteen of the leaders, amonget whom Mr. Parnell, M.P., is named as one of the principal. The leaders of the Land League profess to discountenance sassmination, but they make no secret of their sympathy with these who refuse to fulfil their contractn with their landlords or with such acts as deter landlords from exacting their dues from their tenantry. There can be no doubt that eine° the agitators began the delivery of inflammatory speeches assassinations have been multiplied and the reign of terror intensified. Siam it bemme manifest, however, that the Government were determined to have the laws obeyed the opeeches of agitators have become considerably less fiery. All sensings people will ag eve that the Government, having now satisfied itself that can secure the conviction of offenders, is taking proper steps to teach agitators for lawless acts that they cannot be permitted to foment sedition, and that their followers cannot be allowed to make sacrifices of life and limb with impunity.

The Rev. Father Finegan referred to the fact that though the Board had paid £lO5 14s. ad. for books, they had only received ta 16e. 7d. He, apunently, suggeeted that more ought to be done in dispoeing of books. By dOing so I understand that he has not raised himself in the estimation of eome ot the ratepayers, especially the stationers of the town. These gentlemen complain that the Board should eet iteelf up as a trading concere in books with the money supplied by the ratepayer., and they say that It appear.. If the Board did not Carson, fig whether trades. men prosper or not, but they will take very grod eare they psy thoir School Board rates. What with one rate from the 7,0.1 Boned, another from the School Beard, and the Government taxes, they have about as mush aa they can do in these hard times to make n iving, and yet the bend is to he taken oat of their mouthe by such meass aa these ! It is satirically suggested that the Board had better see if they cannot take up the joiners and building tTadee next, Ito that whenever they want anew school they will be able to build

it themselves. The selling of books is mid to be a Widnes foam of rind eervice more movement, which caused tio much discussion in London a short time ago. There is no doubt that uncomfortable eurroundingn harm anything hut favourable effect on even an eloquent orator and one is, therefore, rather inclines, to sympathise with the members of the Widnes Parliamentary Debating Society, who had, on Wednesday evening last, to adjourn their de- liberations on account of the coinfortless atate of the public hall. Many people see no mason why the building in question ehould not, ender the hands of mine good joiner, he changed into a far more attractive place. Whether it could ever be made too cony or the one in which the members of the Runcorn Parliamentary Debating Society meet is open to dispute. Certainly it would not be a very difficult matter to improve upon its present mate, end something will have , to be done if the members are to be prevented from engaging , some other building.

I understand that the stud) which Mr. Aileen' received at the last meeting of the Wn,lnes Land Board has not acted as an extinguisher in his case, but merely had the effect of adding fuel to the fire already burning. Early in the week Mr. Allcard had an interview with some of the officials of the Board, and asked to can the documents referred to in our columns last week, threatening if he was not shown them he should issue a summons, immediately returnable, under The following sectione of the Public Health Act !—(218 —"The amount of rata which for those purposes it is I necessary to make 'on each pound of such value. And the estimate so made shall forthwith, after being approved of by the be entered in the rate book, and be kept at their office pen to public inspection during office hours thereat but it shall not be deemed part of the rate, nor in any respect affect the validity of the same." (210.)—. Any person interested in, or assessed to any rate under the Art, may inspect the same and any estimate made prvvionsly thereto, and my take copies of, or extracts therefrom, with- out fee or reward. Any parson wbe, having the cuatody of any such estimate or rate, refuses to allow, or does not per- mit such inspection, or such copies or extracts to be Wien, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five pounds." I am told that the result woe that on Friday last, that grille- man and some of those rate-payers who are acting with him, were allowed to see the document.. The report has since been circulated that the following endorsement, is affixed to Ohs last rate, at the and of the rate book, signed on the 12th Inst.,—" We, the undersigned members of the Local Board for the district of Widnes, in the county of Lancaster, do declare that some person on our behalf has examined and compared the several particulars in the respective columns of the foregoing rate, and a valuation list made under the authority of the Union Assemment Committee Ad, 1862,in force in this district ; and the several heredita- ment. are, to the best of our belief, rated according to the sun. of £13,246 16.. 6.1, including £1,270 Se. Id. recoverable arrears of former rates. Dated the 12th day of October. Signed James Cross, Francis Heyes, G. I. Wells, Eustace Carey, James Mcklaughton O'Keeffe." I have been shown an alleged cony of this endorcenienti and I, of course, am puzzled to reconcile the existence of any such enilorsement with the fact that at the last meeting of the Board Mr. Burrow was told the recoverable arrears were only £2.000. If the staleinent be true, a list of these who owe all this money at the time when a 2s. new General District Rate is being laid, would prove very interesting reading. A friend has proffered to give me one, in which, according to his story, which for the credit of the town I hot:le i. not true, one firm owes £340. another £l4O. another £175, another £45, another about £4OO, another £7O, and two firms about £4O each. It is stated that a public meeting is to be called to discuss these statements: but surely they are only idle tales.

-- -- The ratepayer. of Widnes are to be congratulated on the fact of a compromise having been come to in regard to the election of a School Board for that town, as it is stated that a contest would have cost about £l5O. It is said that the nomination of so many independent candidates who are Roman Catholics, after a tacit agreement had been come to, has created. rather unpleasant feeling between them and the leading members of the Nonconformist and Church parties. Last each the meeting of the Runcorn auxiliary at the British and Foreign Bible Society was held, and it may be as well to briefly refer to a subject upon which the Noncon- formists in that town are rather sore. This is that their claims to consideration in anything that may he done for the purpose of furthering the interests of the association is the town, do not at time.. mwt with that attention which they are of opinion they deserve, considering what they have done in the past and what they are doing in the present to help on the work or carrying the Scriptures to the uttermost parts of the globe. Take, for Instance, the various sections of the Wesleyan bode, and especially that particular division known as "the old body," 111Ifi it will be found that their gifts to the society amount to more than all the others pot together. I believe there is a feeling that the Rev. W. Preston, the vicar of Holy Trinity, so arranges matters that he is nearly always the foremost in every movement con. neeted with the association—in fact the modern Agamemnon of it. It may be that this arises very much from thought- lessness, but . .
o Evil Is wrought by want of thought As wel,a‘rf,nt of hesrt... • •

--...-. --..„ and a gentleman with the mature judgment and education of Mr. Preston ought to consider that his Nonconformist brethren have possibly aa fine sensibilities under their black coats as he under his black gown. In a great work like that of multiplying copra. of the Word of God, there ought not to be any seeming preference for one particular mration of the great Protestant family; but I fear, from what I have been told, that n similar cause of offence has been given in other towns. Offences "must needs come," but the Book says woe unto that man by whom they come. As some proof that thou Non. celpformists who feel ?slightly irritated on this subject ItsA ground for complaint, I may mention that at the anneal meeting of the auxiliary last week the Rey. Canon Barclay presided, the Rev. W. Preston read the report, the gentleman who attended Ma deputation was a Churchman, and the only duty—one of vast weight certainly t—imposed upon the superintendent of the Wmleyan Methediet body (Mr. Nowell) was to move a rote of thanks. I should be sorry to take any part in causing disunion rather than union amongst the Christians of the town, but [have been reqnested to draw attention to this subject. Why should not repre- -1 sentatiyes from every church in Rthcorn find a place on a platform upon which the Calvinist may unite with the greatest admirer of Anninius, anti the most Latitudinarian may grasp hands with the greatest Ritualist? In some towns I believe it is the custom to send two deputations to such • meeting, urea Churchman and the other a Noncoe.l formist. The leading spirit in connection with the latter , party in Runcorn would emphatically be considered Mr. John Simpson, but he does not seem to hare attended the meeting, though this may poseibly be explained by the fact he liver out of town. This, however. can hardly, on second thoughts, he considered a sufficient excuse, as he is nearly I invariably found on the platform at any gathering of his 1 co-religionists in that town. In concluding my brief refer. ence to the subject, I may refer to the fact that the meeting , was not even advertised, and it was held in the ante-room of the Public Hall. How ia it to be retracted that the auxiliary . can become healthy when just to avoid the paltry charge for 1• brief newspaper announcement the public are left coin. paratiyely in the dark as to such • meeting being held ?

There are few towns of the sine where the number of ' juvenile offenders is eo great as in Widnes. Hardly a month passes without some youngster or other being com- mitted to an industrial school, or reformatory; and one would almost be inclined to think there was some Fagin like the one immortalised by Dickene in " Oliver Twist," who : was secretly training city Arabs for thieving. This state of things &Aye very little for the attention paid to the habits of lads by some Widnes parents ; and it is high time the mini.: tore, but more especially the priests of the town, he out FLACCUS, on this subject.

There was a fair at, tendance of members on both sides of the House, and a fair sprinkling of visitors in the Stnsngers' Gallery. The Speaker took his seat shortly after eight o'clock ; and, the House having been called to order, the member tor Stoko asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether it w. not • fact that from the returns on the table a decrease WAS shown in the Revenne returns for the year ending 30th September of £752,739, as compared with the preceding year of the late Government. —The Chancellor of the Ex- chequer repli.d that it was true the revenue returns showed a net d.reaw, but be might add that whilst thin was so, the returne for the past quarter shonlad a net increase of £405,000, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. Thereon. every indication that the present quarter weuld also stow an increase. The returns had evidenced great elasticity and improvement, and there was every reason to believe the improvement would centinue.—The Attorney General introduced a bill to amend the aystem of secret vloting.—The delete wa, adjourned on the motion of the hon. member for Lincoln.—ln the absence of the hon. member for Dever, the member for Devizes moved "That this Honse regards with coneern the statement of the Chief Secretary for Ireland that her Majesty's Government do not intend to introduce any measure for the preservation of order and the e.urity of life in Ireland."—A very animated debate followed, which was taken part in by the meinbers for Guildford, Edinburgh, Dover (who came ffi at a later part of the discussion). Halifax, Stoke, the Attorney General, the President of the Board of Trade,and the Foreign Secretary.—The adjournment of the debate was moved by the Home Secretary.—The member for Devisee gore notice that at the next sitting of the House he would ask the Vice- President of the Council "seeing that Her Majesty's Go- vernment deny the existence of Turkey as a European power, will he intern, the House whether he has given in. structinne to her Majesty's inspectors of elementary schools not to question pupil teachers and scholars upon the geography of Turkey, as given intent books ased in the eaid school, sad whether he will inform the Moose what power is now in possession of the .southern part of the country, previously occupied by the Turks, and under the govern- ment and rule of the Sultan of Turkey."—The member for Bedford gave notice that be world ask the Home Secretary if his latent'an had been called to the fact that Jesuits and other eccleeiastica expelled from F.ance and Germany are making this country their rendezvous, and whether the Government is prepared to take any steps to prevent their becoming a pest to this land, as they have been to the countries from which they have been expelled.—The House them adjourned. - - . -

When he saw the little book Father Turner tent him a short time ago, and found there iicrustate," he thought really that wee a nice word, and it reminded him of those times in the church's history, when people were righting for the holy cause, and shedding their blood, and sacrificing everything, and even giving their lives for the great came. then he thought of doing some- thing to put before them. He would tell them e little of th. ern/rules, because then they would sec there woe a parallel: I rhe reverend genUenian here gave an interesting and explanatory history of the crusades, showing how the Christians eucceedell in obtaining possesaion of the Holy City In spite of the immense difficulties they bad to encounter.) Having given them a skoteh of the elkurch'e hirtory he asked them if it were not iressiblo in those day, to have a little of that enthusiasm, especially if they looked on the enemy they had to fight against, an enemy that did an much berm as the Turk. did to the Cruraders. 08.000 men, Cardinal Manning had said, died every year in this country in consequence of drunkenness. Whilst they fought against it they fought for morality, for as it increased morality decreased ; whilst they fought It they fought for immortality and for the cause of Christ, to whom all those souls belonged, for the cause of God hhnself, on whom their great hopes of happiness and peace were founded. I)id they not feel they were fighting for a great and holy muse? Let them, then, givo Chore,, bode mind and strength to it. What they must do that night was to unfurl and hold high the banner of temperance, and say " It is Ood's will, it is God's will. (Loud applause.) The MAYOR tom to suggest a hearty voto of thanks to the rev. gentleman, which he fully deserved for three reasons lie had crone among them that night from a distance, although much engaged, to give at such an admirable lecture. He bad shown great interest in them and the people of St. Helem, and lost ensigns that they should ho. sohon people and advance in °ono wav possible. And another reason Cu,, he was 000 01 the Fact°, who had been driven from their own coantry. He was among them noise • stranger, tecause a Catholic priest nais never a stranger amonget a Catholic audience. (Applause.) Ile was driven from his cum country not by the Catholics or the people to whom the Fathers bet rendered such benefit, but by those high in authority. He would per see the thy when Germany would be glad to receive beck thnne (term:. Fathers with open arms. (Cheers were here given for Father liattlitt, who called for cheers for the rev. president.) The rev. Cameras having thanked all who had taken part in the proceedings, announced that the et at tenni. would be held in a month's time, and that it was intended to have reunions every menth. Maclean, of Longton, who is very popular in St. Helene, not only amongst the Church people but also amongst the Nonconformists, preached in the evening to a crowded congregation. On Thursday night, the Bishop of Liverpool occupied the pulpit. The church was crowded to hear the new bishop. The Rev, Dr. Carr read the lesson, and the Rev. Mermargen the prayers. The church Wa3 beautifully decorated for the occasion. Cwrecn MISSIONARY Funetwrw.—Last Sunday two ser- mons were preached in Wharton Church, W.insford, on behalf of the above society, in the morning by the Rev. R. painter, MA, late missionary in China; in the evening by the Rev. J. Caley, M A., missionary from Travancore radii. Similar services were held at Christ Church. Winsford, when the Rev. E. Woodyart, M.A. nicer of St. John's. Over, preached in the morning, and the Rev. R. Palmer ofliciated St the evening service. This rev. gentleman also gay° the address at a children's service in Christ Church on Sunday afternoon: as well as at the missionary meeting in Wharton ' school, on Monday evening. Collections OR each occasion were made, and amount to • good round sum.

The MATO. mid that as tkis sass the last meeting of the year of the Highway Committee he begged to propose that thanks be given to the chairman and the deputy-chairman for their servicee during the year. It might be said that committee had spent a large amount, and that the rates bad been incremed in consequeace. I reply to that there was no doubt that money had lwen spent, end the only fault that could be attribut,:d to that commit. was that they had gone a little too tent, but no one could deny the town pre- sented • very different appearance to what it did snow time ago. (Hear, hear, from alrnoat all the committee, eimulta- neouely.) He bad no hesitation in /laying, and it was con- tinually observed by many who knew St. Helens, that it did present a much more attractive appearance. He would say I further that the ratepayers, although they bad to pay for it, thought they had got value for their money. It reminded I him of a circninstance which took place at the Town Hall some year. ago in his younger day,, when a very important po'l took place. A person remarkable for her saving pro- pensities was brought up to vote in favour of the church rate,', 3nd when ehe waa asked to vote in favour of that she mid emphatimily," Mesa certtioly; I shall do so because I have greet respect for the church I belong to and was brought up in." Another person near her said," Mary, will von vote to per?" "No, that I won't" WAS the reply. Laughter.) So that people in the town will be very glad to hare new street., still It tem a very unpleasant thing when the bill WAS to be paid. He hoped they would be able in tire course of the next twelve months to reduce the amount • of the deficiency considerably, end that, next year they may be able ta say they had learnt a lesson and that they had . kept within limits. Theo the vMe-chairman bad left his business to come there, and must very often suffer in • monebtry point of view. He begged lo move that • vote of • thanks be tendered to those gentlemen. Mr. Mchecutas seconded the leonine, and remarked that It was a pleisure to serve under the chairman, and vice- chairman of that committee. They had several committees with its chairman, but no one surpassed the chairman of the Highways Committee. They had got on renurkably well and looking hick nine or ten years the time when he came to St. Helens, he could at present see marked difference in the town. Of course there had been a great.deat of money spent, hut in most cases it bad been pent wisely and would be better in the end. (Applause.) he motion having been carried, he CHAIRMAN thanked them for the teeny kind things that had been coil about him personally, and also what had been anid about the c iminittee. Of course MeV were a spending mmmittee, and it was their business to look after the streets mid roads. At times, ratepayers and others had remarked to him about the very fine condition and beautiful state of the town, nod the improvements that had been made. He thought the money had been spent wisely.
